subject: math
description: Students distinguish statistical questions from non-statistical questions. A statistical question is one that anticipates variability in the data used to answer it, so its answer comes from a distribution of values gathered across many individuals or repeated observations. A non-statistical question has a single, fixed answer with no variability. Students must classify questions, explain WHY a question is or is not statistical (by pointing to whether the answers would vary), and revise a non-statistical question into a statistical one.
subSkills: Define a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the answers
Classify a given question as statistical or non-statistical
Justify the classification by reasoning about whether the answers would vary across individuals or observations
Identify the population or group whose variability a statistical question investigates
Distinguish a question about a single individual or fact (no variability) from a question about a group (variability expected)
Rewrite a non-statistical question so that it anticipates variability
Match a statistical question to the kind of data and the type of answer (a distribution or summary) it would produce

problemArchetypes.name: Classify a single question
problemArchetypes.example: Is the question 'How tall are the students in my 6th grade class?' statistical or not statistical? Answer: Statistical, because heights vary from student to student, so the answers form a distribution.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the non-statistical question from a set
problemArchetypes.example: Which of these is NOT a statistical question? 'How old is the principal of our school?' has one fixed answer, so it is not statistical, while the others ask about a varying group.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain the reasoning
problemArchetypes.example: Explain why 'How many minutes did each student in the class spend on homework last night?' is a statistical question. Answer: Different students spent different amounts of time, so the answers vary and form a distribution.

problemArchetypes.name: Revise a non-statistical question into a statistical one
problemArchetypes.example: Rewrite the non-statistical question 'How many pages are in my math textbook?' as a statistical question. Sample answer: 'How many pages are in the math textbooks used across the 6th grade?'

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the population and the data collected
problemArchetypes.example: For the statistical question 'What are the daily high temperatures in our town this month?', the population is the set of days this month and the data are the recorded high temperatures, which vary day to day.

problemArchetypes.name: Single-fact vs group with a numerical twist
problemArchetypes.example: Decide whether 'What was the score of yesterday's basketball game?' (one fixed result, not statistical) versus 'What were the scores of our team's games this season?' (scores vary game to game, statistical).

Easy.description: Clear-cut single classification. The question is obviously about one fixed fact (not statistical) or obviously about a varying group (statistical), with everyday contexts. Student only labels statistical vs not statistical.
constraints: One question to classify, with an unambiguous answer
Non-statistical examples are about one specific person, object, or fact ('How old am I?', 'How many wheels are on a bicycle?')
Statistical examples obviously survey a group ('How tall are the students in our class?')
No revision or population identification required
Familiar contexts: classroom, home, sports, pets

Medium.description: Requires justification or discrimination between similar-looking questions. Student must explain WHY using the idea of variability, or pick the statistical/non-statistical item from a set where the surface wording is close. May ask the student to name the group whose answers vary.
constraints: Student must give a reason that references variability or a single fixed answer, not just a label
Distractor questions look numerical but have a single answer (e.g., counting a fixed quantity) to test the misconception that 'numbers make it statistical'
May require identifying the population or the data that would be collected
Questions about 'how many' that are non-statistical (one fixed count) are contrasted with 'how many ... each' that are statistical

Hard.description: Multi-step or generative. Student revises a non-statistical question into a statistical one (or vice versa), or evaluates a flawed classification and corrects the reasoning, or matches a statistical question to the distribution of data it produces. Requires producing language, not just selecting it.
constraints: Student rewrites a question to add or remove anticipated variability
Or student critiques another student's incorrect classification and explains the error
Or student determines what data would be collected and whether the answer is a single value or a distribution
Contexts may be less familiar (weather, populations, measurement over time) and wording is deliberately subtle

difficultyRubric._tierSplitNote: This standard is a single ramped worksheet (single = 15), not a tier1/tier2 pair. The concept has one core skill (classify by anticipated variability) that ramps from labeling (Easy) to justifying/discriminating (Medium) to revising/critiquing (Hard). If it were ever split, tier1 would cover Easy-to-Medium classification and justification, and tier2 would cover Medium-to-Hard revision, critique, and population/data identification.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Any question that contains a number or asks 'how many' is statistical
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'How many days are in a week?' or 'How many legs does a spider have?' as statistical because it involves a number, ignoring that the answer is a single fixed value with no variability

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A question about one specific individual is statistical because it is about a person
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'How tall is our teacher?' as statistical, confusing 'about a person' with 'anticipates variability'; one teacher has one height, so there is no variability

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A statistical question must produce one correct summary number, so questions with a single answer are statistical
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasons that because you can compute an average there is only one answer, so the question is not statistical, reversing the definition (variability in the DATA, not in the final summary, is what matters)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A question is statistical only if it explicitly uses the words 'average', 'mean', or 'data'
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'How many pets does each student in the class have?' as not statistical because it does not say 'average', overlooking that the per-student answers vary

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A yes/no or opinion question can never be statistical
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'Do the students in our grade like pizza?' as not statistical, missing that responses vary across students and form a distribution

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A question about a group of objects is non-statistical if the objects seem identical
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'What are the weights of the apples in this basket?' as not statistical, assuming the apples are the same when in fact their weights vary

_comment_itemCounts: Single ramped worksheet (15 items, Easy->Hard). Lesson 5 worked examples + 5 practice. Quiz 8 multiple-choice. tier1/tier2 listed for schema completeness but not used for this standard.
